answer: POST /heartbeat, called periodically by every client; each call marks whichever user is authenticated on that request as alive ('I am alive').
evidence: Ch 2.3: 'The endpoint is POST /heartbeat. Each call marks whichever user is authenticated on that request as alive.'

answer: A client can announce coming online but can't reliably announce going offline: a crash, dead battery or pulled plug sends no offline call, so the UI keeps showing the user online (stale dot). You aren't in control of the moment the device dies, so heartbeats must be periodic.
evidence: Ch 2.4: 'You can tell the server when you come online; you can't promise a call just before the device dies ... This fundamental limitation is why heartbeats must be periodic.'

answer: When the backend receives no heartbeat for 'long enough'. That is subjective business logic configured per system (could be 10 minutes, 10 seconds or a minute); this design uses 30 seconds of silence with a heartbeat every 10 seconds.
evidence: Ch 2.4: '“Long enough” is subjective ... For one system it might be 10 minutes ... others 10 seconds or a minute. This design marks a user offline after 30 seconds of silence, with clients sending a heartbeat every 10 seconds.'

answer: Instead of a boolean, store the time the last heartbeat was received: table pulse(user_id, last_heartbeat), time as epoch seconds; every POST /heartbeat updates that user's row (in practice an upsert, since the first beat has no row).
evidence: Ch 2.5: 'instead of a boolean, store the time at which the last heartbeat was received. The table is pulse(user_id, last_heartbeat), and every POST /heartbeat updates that user's row.'

answer: Rule 1: no entry for the user -> offline (never came online). Rule 2: entry exists but last_heartbeat is older than now - 30 seconds -> offline. Otherwise -> online. Same rules for every ID in a batch call.
evidence: Ch 2.5: 'Rule 1: if there is no entry for a user, return offline ... Rule 2: ... older than now minus 30 seconds ... return offline. Otherwise the user is online.'

answer: Every 10 seconds.

answer: The user only sees online or offline, so treat absence of an entry as offline: a row exists only for online users. Every heartbeat resets a 30-second timer and the entry is deleted when it runs out, so number of entries = users online at that moment, cutting rows significantly.
evidence: Ch 2.7: 'treat the absence of an entry as offline. A row exists only for a user who is online ... The number of entries then equals the number of users online at that moment.'

answer: Offload the deletion to the datastore: use a database that natively expires entries (key-value access plus TTL), instead of reinventing the wheel. Redis and DynamoDB.
evidence: Ch 2.8: 'can we not offload this to our datastore? ... a database with key-value access plus expiration ... Two very common ones are Redis and DynamoDB.'

answer: Each heartbeat sets the user's entry with a 30-second TTL, moving the expiration forward; after 30 s without a heartbeat the database deletes it. Entry exists -> online, absent -> offline. Caveats: in Redis each write must re-send the TTL (SET user:<id> 1 EX 30), since plain SET clears expiry and the key would never expire; DynamoDB TTL deletes 'typically within a few days', so store expires_at = now+30 and treat expires_at < now as offline.
evidence: Ch 2.8: 'On every heartbeat, set the user's entry ... with a TTL of 30 seconds ... every heartbeat moves the expiration time forward ... If the entry exists, the user is online' and 'More precisely' note.

answer: Because Redis lets you hold persistent connections, giving extremely low latency, whereas DynamoDB is stateless (no persistent connections). answer: Five trips as the lecture counts: three-way handshake to set up and two-way teardown (more in reality with DB login and TLS). It matters because each heartbeat is a micro update (one row by primary key), so most time goes into establishing the TCP connection: the biggest bottleneck; the DB also spends CPU, bandwidth, buffers (and a process in PostgreSQL) to accept it.
evidence: Ch 4.2: 'three-way handshake; closing it takes a two-way teardown. That is five network trips for every single call ... most of the time goes into establishing the TCP connection, the biggest performance bottleneck in this design.'

answer: Instead of closing each connection after its query, keep a set of connections open between the server and the database and reuse them (e.g. the API server opens three at startup and uses any free one for any query).
evidence: Ch 4.3: 'Connection pooling means: instead of closing each connection after its query, keep a set of connections open between the server and the database and reuse them.'

answer: Because the database is spared the connection work: reading handshake packets, CPU and network (class narrowed it to 'not really memory, but CPU and network'; the page adds memory is part of it too: per-connection threads/buffers/processes). With one-row micro updates that dramatically reduces its load.
evidence: Ch 4.3: 'the load on the database drops, even though the number of queries stays exactly the same. The database is spared the connection work, mainly CPU and network ... Memory is part of the saving too'

answer: API calls become much faster; load on the database drops (same queries); i.e. faster responses for users, DB freed to run other queries, and a smaller infrastructure bill. Big gain for micro updates.
evidence: Ch 4.3: 'That gives two benefits. The API call becomes much faster. And the load on the database drops ... faster responses for users, a database freed up to run other queries, and a smaller infrastructure bill.'

answer: Two options: wait until a running query releases a connection, or establish a new TCP connection, fire the query and add it to the pool (pool stretches, e.g. 3 -> 4), up to the configured maximum. At the max (e.g. 100) request 101 waits for a release, up to a timeout (HikariCP connectionTimeout 30 s default, then error).
evidence: Ch 4.5: 'The first is to wait ... The second ... establish a new TCP connection, fire the query, and add that connection to the pool ... If all 100 are in use, request 101 waits'

answer: Max: unbounded stretching under millions of requests would grow the pool without limit, and every database has a TCP connection limit; hundreds of servers each with 100 would exceed it (Postgres default max_connections ~100). Idle TTL: the pool should close connections nobody uses (e.g. idle 10 minutes) so a server holds fewer connections on the DB; neither too short (long queries) nor too long (unused connections hog slots).
evidence: Ch 4.5: 'Stretching without a limit is a problem ... Every database has a limit on the number of TCP connections ... it is also the pool's job to close connections nobody is using. You configure a TTL per connection'

answer: No, it is not a separate service/process; it's a simple library inside the API server. At boot it creates several DB connection objects and puts them in a blocking queue; a caller pops one (waiting if none is free) and puts it back after use. (A central pooler like PgBouncer/RDS Proxy is a separate service, for a different problem.)
evidence: Ch 4.4: 'A connection pool is not one. It is a simple library running inside the api server ... creates several database connection objects and puts them in a blocking queue.'

answer: Massive boost when updates are micro (one row by primary key, straight to a B+ tree leaf). For a big SQL query, the query itself runs long enough to outweigh what the pool saves.
evidence: Ch 4.3: 'For a big SQL query it is different: the query itself runs long enough to outweigh what the pool saves. The pool's big win comes when the updates are micro.'

answer: Failure detection in a distributed system: nodes send heartbeats to a central tracker, and a node whose heartbeats stop is down (e.g. building your own AWS from EC2 machines, or a load balancer detecting dead backends).

answer: It waits, retrying, and succeeds only when an existing server terminates one of its connections. In practice the DB refuses with an error and the pool waits only up to its timeout (30 s default in HikariCP), so requests fail rather than hang. Fix: scale the database up (vertical) or shard.
evidence: Ch 4.5: 'A new server that can't get a connection waits, retrying, and succeeds only when an existing server terminates one of its connections. In practice ... Requests on that new server fail rather than hang'; Ch 4.6 'Then you scale the database up'

answer: The maximum number of connections it can handle. The DB's size depends on the number of concurrent queries you fire; the concurrency you want decides how many concurrent connections it must handle. Beyond the limit: scale vertically or shard.
evidence: Ch 4.6: 'The size of the database depends on the number of concurrent queries ... the most common bottleneck of a database in most cases is the maximum number of connections it can handle'

answer: As argued: most engines store data as a B+ tree; hard delete removes the entry, unbalancing the tree, so the engine spends CPU rebalancing; soft delete only updates a column, no rebalancing. Caveat: engines actually defer deletes (InnoDB purge, Postgres VACUUM), merge pages only below ~50% fill, and an update is still a write, so the saving is smaller; choose soft delete for recovery/archival/audit.
evidence: Ch 5.3: 'easy on the database engine (no tree re-balancing)' and 'More precisely' note.

answer: VARCHAR (short text) stays inline with the other columns in the row; LONGTEXT is stored in a separate location on disk with only a reference in the row, so reading it takes two disk calls. (Engines vary: InnoDB moves off-page only if the row doesn't fit; PostgreSQL TOAST moves any wide value past ~2 kB.)
evidence: Ch 5.6: 'A short text column (VARCHAR) stays inline ... A long text column (LONGTEXT) is stored ... in a separate location on disk ... the row keeps only a reference'

answer: Short: email, bio, first name, last name (VARCHAR). Long: blog body, long comments. Hard limits too (InnoDB ~8 KB in-page, MySQL 65,535 bytes).
evidence: Ch 5.6: 'Email, bio, first name and last name are short text ... A blog body or a long comment is long text ... the length of a row has to be limited.'
